{{Short description|Statistical characterization of distribution functions}}
{{Orphan|date=July 2026}}

In [[probability theory]] and [[statistics]], the '''dispersion function''' is a functional that characterizes a [[probability distribution]] by measuring the expected absolute deviation of a random variable from any given point. It was introduced by J. Muñoz-Pérez and A. Sánchez-Gómez in 1990 as a tool for studying [[statistical dispersion]] and inducing a partial ordering of distributions.<ref name="Munoz1990">{{cite journal |last1=Muñoz-Pérez |first1=J. |last2=Sánchez-Gómez |first2=A. |title=A characterization of the distribution function: The dispersion function |journal=Statistics & Probability Letters |date=1990 |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=235–239 |doi=10.1016/0167-7152(90)90080-Q}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Let <math>X</math> be a real-valued [[random variable]] with a finite expectation (<math>X \in \mathcal{L}_1</math>). The '''dispersion function''' <math>D_X(u)</math> is defined as the absolute moment of order <math>r=1</math> of the random variable <math>X</math> with respect to <math>u</math>:<ref name="Munoz1990" />

<math display="block">D_X(u) = E|X - u|, \quad \forall u \in \mathbb{R}</math>

== Characterization of the distribution ==
The dispersion function uniquely determines the [[cumulative distribution function]] (CDF) of <math>X</math>. If <math>C_F</math> is the set of continuity points of <math>F_X</math>, the distribution function can be recovered via the derivative of the dispersion function:<ref name="Munoz1990" />

<math display="block">F_X(u) = \frac{1}{2}(D_X'(u) + 1)</math>

== Properties ==
The dispersion function has the following properties:<ref name="Munoz1990" />
* '''Convexity''': <math>D_X</math> is a [[convex function]] on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>.
* '''Differentiability''': It is differentiable, and its derivative <math>D_X'</math> has at most a countable number of discontinuity points.
* '''Asymptotic behavior of the derivative''': The limits of the derivative are <math>\lim_{x \to \infty} D_X'(x) = 1</math> and <math>\lim_{x \to -\infty} D_X'(x) = -1</math>.
* '''Mean relationship''': The limits involving the mean <math>EX</math> are given by <math>\lim_{x \to \infty} [D_X(x) - x] = -EX</math> and <math>\lim_{x \to -\infty} [D_X(x) + x] = EX</math>.

== Relation to Variance ==
For a random variable with finite variance <math>\sigma^2</math>, the <math>L_1</math>-distance between its dispersion function and the dispersion function of the degenerate random variable at its mean (<math>D_{EX}(u) = |EX - u|</math>) is exactly the variance:<ref name="Munoz1990" />

<math display="block">\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} |D_X(u) - D_{EX}(u)| du = \sigma^2</math>

== Dispersive Ordering ==
In the study of [[stochastic orders]], the dispersion function provides a necessary and sufficient condition for the dispersive ordering. This concept builds upon earlier work by Bickel and Lehmann regarding descriptive statistics for non-parametric models.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bickel |first1=P.J. |last2=Lehmann |first2=E.L. |title=Descriptive statistics for non-parametric models. III. Dispersion |journal=Annals of Statistics |date=1976 |volume=4 |issue=6 |pages=1139–1158 |doi=10.1214/aos/1176343650}}</ref> According to Shaked and Shanthikumar,<ref name="Shaked2007">{{cite book |last1=Shaked |first1=Moshe |last2=Shanthikumar |first2=J. George |title=Stochastic Orders |date=2007 |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-0-387-32915-4 |series=Springer Series in Statistics}}</ref> this characterization allows for the comparison of distributions even when they have the same finite support, such as comparing a [[continuous uniform distribution]] to a [[triangular distribution]] (Simpson's distribution).

== Generalizations ==
A generalized '''dispersion function of order p''' is defined as the <math>L_p</math>-distance between the [[quantile function]] <math>Q_X</math> and the quantile function of a degenerate variable at <math>u</math>:<ref name="Munoz1990" />

<math display="block">D_X(u,p) = \left( \int_{0}^{1} [Q_X(t) - u]^p d\Lambda(t) \right)^{1/p}</math>

where <math>\Lambda</math> is a probability distribution on <math>(0,1)</math> and <math>p</math> is any positive number.
